strengths: Unifying benchmarking attempts for protein generative models is an extremely important open challenge.

Studying various common evaluation metrics systematically and in a controlled setup is impactful because it can inform future developments of new methods and allow researchers to benchmark their models in a more convincing way.
The problem is motivated nicely and grounded in related works.
The paper addresses three dimensions of generative model evaluation: quality, diversity, and distributional similarity.
It identifies at least two axes along which evaluation metrics should be assessed: robustness vs sensitivity and reliability vs computational efficiency.
Together these cover most practically relevant aspects of model evaluation in this space.

The paper's background section and motivation is extremely strong. The need for reliable evaluation metrics for protein generation is convincing and some of the metrics used in the literature are clearly outlined.
The controlled experiments are well thought out and provide some useful information about the quality of the metrics.
The authors perform a rigorous set of experiments and the provided practical recommendations could be useful to the community.
Evaluation of robustness to several protein sequence generation metrics.

Originality: A systematic analysis of metric variability with protein sequence diversity is a good idea and I would recommend the authors to build on it, but incorporate several improvements: Instead of uniform probabilities for mutations it might be more meaningful to use PAM or BLOSUM matrices.

Significance: The authors correctly emphasize that there is no gold-standard in the field of generative protein models on what constitutes a "good" protein. The topic is worth being addressed, although I don't think that this work provides a significant contribution.
weaknesses: The clarity of the presentation of their results can be improved; the arguments are sometimes difficult to follow.

The experimental results section could be restructured so that each subsection (quality, diversity and distribution similarity) systematically analyses different available metrics regarding their (1) robustness-sensitivity trade-off, and (2) reliability-efficiency trade-off, with a clear quantitative criterion and identical structure.
The current discussion sometimes mixes empirically supported findings with intuition-derived arguments.

In the background section it is confusing that most of the time the paper discusses three key axes of model performance (quality, diversity, distribution similarity) but Section 2.2 talks about an alternative set of objectives (fidelity, diversity, novelty).
The paper introduces "Interpretability" in Section 2.3 but does not discuss this aspect in the Results section.

The scope of the work is unclear; it only covers generative models for amino acid sequences as opposed to backbone structures, and the discussion about self-consistency seems unnecessarily detailed given it is used only once later on (scPerplexity metric).
Readers may be misled to think the paper discusses both sequence and structure generative models because self-consistency is primarily used in the evaluation of structure design methods (e.g., [1]).

The analysis of diversity metrics (Section 4.3) is extremely short, and it is unclear whether Figure 3 provides information about the sensitivity or robustness of the Cluster Density metric; the absence of a comparison with alternative approaches additionally makes it hard to interpret the results.

Some claims lack empirical support; for instance, Figure 9 shows notable differences between AlphaFold2 and ESMFold but the paper does not explore how sensitive and robust each method is to sample quality differences.
The paper states that simple diversity metrics lack discriminative power but does not discuss any examples in the analysis in Section 4.3.

The paper mentions intrinsically disordered regions as a potential stumbling block for the pLDDT metric, but provides no empirical data to confirm whether pLDDT has better discriminative power than alternative metrics in those cases.
Statements about computational efficiency are never quantified; concrete run times are missing, preventing readers from assessing the reliability‑efficiency trade‑off.

The main weakness comes from evaluating the metrics in a controlled and synthetic setting; quality metrics are evaluated on proteins which the models (such as ESMFold) are trained on, so it is unclear whether these metrics generalize to unseen proteins or correlate with experimental results.

It is not clear how the methods differ in terms of computational efficiency; scPerplexity is said to be expensive but no timing comparison is provided, and the claimed rapid evaluation metrics lack quantitative runtime information.
The work contains no technical novelty or new results; the presentation quality is low and the insights are not novel enough for acceptance.
The work claims to evaluate protein generative models but ignores protein structure generative models such as RFdiffusion [1] and Chroma [2]; this is a major omission.

There are no benchmarks of generative models; experiments are conducted on artificial perturbations of known sequences and on a curated set of sequences from five protein families, making the insights unconvincing.
Metrics are only useful if they correspond to success in downstream applications; the metrics used are not associated with downstream success and are merely auxiliary.
The noise perturbations are artificial; it is unclear whether randomly mutating 5‑30% of the sequence reflects a realistic failure mode or common occurrence in existing protein generative models.
Novelty is mentioned as an important consideration but no novelty metrics are presented or discussed.
Only using five protein families is far too small of an evaluation set, and the reference to "real‑world generated data" is ambiguous.
Section 4.3 on diversity metric analysis is weak; the trend in Figure 3 reflects expected behavior of the 50% and 95% sequence similarity threshold and provides no new insight.
Figures 2 and 3 show that more noise leads to all metrics becoming worse, which is expected and offers no indication of how this transfers to commonly used protein generative models.

Section 4.4 is also weak on insights; the graphs are expected by changing the noise and RBG kernel width, and the claims are too general to be useful for specific downstream applications such as binder design.
The paper lacks a ranking of protein sequence generative models such as ESM2, ProGen, and T5 with the presented metrics.

The motivation of diversity in the absence of training data is confusing; the paper should discuss the non‑bijective nature of the sequence‑structure relationship and the complexity of diversity in the solution space.
The authors mention structural stability as a measure of a "good" protein but do not evaluate this property in the work.
Mathematical notations (especially under "self‑consistency") are overly complicated and are not used elsewhere in the paper.
Fidelity metrics do not address structural fidelity in terms of structural similarity (e.g., TM‑score or RMSE) for forward folding, nor self‑consistency TM for inverse folding.
Metrics should be split for different generative model types and approaches (e.g., sequence‑based LLMs vs. inverse folding models).

Metrics claimed to be interpretable (e.g., perplexity, pseudo‑perplexity) are not truly interpretable; more interpretable metrics such as edit distance or structure consistency (e.g., TM‑score) should be considered.
The diversity definition of cluster density at 50% and 95% is interesting but should be compared to more commonly adopted diversity metrics such as edit distance and pairwise distances.
The systematic perturbation of amino acid sequences using uniform transition probabilities is unrealistic; using BLOSUM or PAM matrices would be more meaningful.
The paper lacks an actual application to generative models; it should include experiments with inverse folding models (e.g., ESMIF or ProteinMPNN) and realistic decoding strategies.
Random perturbations do not create meaningful biological diversity and simply degrade quality; Figures 2 and 4 therefore show obvious trends (more noise leads to worse quality/fidelity metrics).
Citation style is unfriendly and should be reviewed.
Supplementary figures are not marked as such (e.g., Figure 9).
Figure 8 is missing.
